topic: S4 Embodied scenario, infrastructure assignment: how fast robots plus AI can compress the build time of data centers, power plants and grid, semiconductor fabs, factories, housing, roads and bridges, and which parts of a build are labor-bound versus equipment-, materials-, permit-, physics- and capital-bound (research date 2026-10-07)
key_findings: The speed frontier for infrastructure is already set by organization, capital and permitting, not by robots. xAI built Colossus 1 (~300 MW) in 122 days and took Colossus 2 from site purchase (Mar 7 2025) to ~200 MW of cooling in ~5.5 months, with human crews, by reusing industrial shells and running mobile gas turbines and Megapacks ahead of the grid (SemiAnalysis, Sep 2025). Epoch puts typical construction-start-to-1 GW at 1-4 years. Best practice is therefore already 3-12x faster than typical without robots; robotics mainly raises how many such sites can run at once (aggregate GW per year), not how fast one site can go.

In the United States the longest poles are institutional queues and equipment queues, which robots do not touch directly: median generator interconnection request-to-operation was 61 months for projects built in 2025, up from 22 months in 2008 (LBNL Queued Up 2026); a 100 MW load connection in Northern Virginia waits ~7 years and ~4 years nationally (JLL 2026, reported); an interregional line took ~18 years (SunZia, 2008 to Jun 2026); FHWA's estimate for a major highway is 9-19 years planning-to-construction; median EIS was 2.2 years in 2024 (CEQ).

Equipment lead times are queues, and lead time = backlog / throughput. Robots raise throughput, but an embodied-AI boom raises the backlog at the same time. GE Vernova had 116 GW of gas equipment under contract or slot reservation in Q2 2026 against ~20 GW/yr of output (≈5.8 years of output), heavy-duty lead times of ~3 years and only ~10 GW open across 2029-2030; generator step-up transformer demand rose 274% from 2019 to 2025 (Wood Mackenzie via pv magazine) with large units at 128-144 weeks and up to 4 years. Under S4, equipment lead times are unlikely to fall before robot-staffed factory capacity outruns demand, which we date after 2030.

Amdahl applied to infrastructure: field labor is ~25% of the critical path of a U.S. grid-connected project and ~40% of a permissive or behind-the-meter one (estimate). With S4 field-labor speedups of 1.4x (average project) to 2x (leading edge) by 2031, a U.S. grid-connected build is 21-28% shorter versus 19% under S3; a permissive build is 21-31% shorter. By 2035 (labor 3-4x, equipment 1.6-2x) the U.S. case is 38-45% shorter and the permissive case 45-54%. Even with labor and equipment free, institutions and physics cap the 2031 U.S. case at ~56% shorter. Robotics adds only ~2-9 points over S3 by 2031.

Construction is the sector that has most resisted mechanization. Goolsbee and Syverson (NBER w30845) document a decades-long productivity decline; secondary coverage puts 2020 value added per worker ~40% below 1970, and a Goldman-based estimate finds -30% over 1970-2024 while economy-wide labor productivity more than doubled. The causes they point to (site uniqueness, fragmentation, market frictions, regulation) also slow robot adoption, so S4 should not assume construction adopts at factory speed.

Construction robotics in October 2026 is real but single-task and small: Komatsu commissioned its 1,000th autonomous ultra-class haul truck in Apr 2026, 18 years after commercial launch (fleet growth ~18%/yr since Feb 2024, doubling ~4 years) in the most structured outdoor setting there is; Bedrock Robotics ($350M raised) went operator-free on three live U.S. sites on Aug 17 2026; Built Robotics pile drivers claim ~300 piles/day with a two-person crew versus ~100 conventionally; Dusty claims 100-300M sq ft of layout; Canvas (bought by JLG, Jan 2026) cuts drywall finishing from ~5 days to ~2; Hilti Jaibot claims 500 overhead holes/day; ICON has ~250 printed structures in nine years and cut 25% of staff in 2025. These are 2-4x gains on narrow activities that are each a small slice of the critical path.

General-purpose (humanoid) labor is not on construction sites yet. Shipments were ~13-16k in 2025 and ~19k in H1 2026, ~65% for entertainment, education, research and data collection; Boston Dynamics reportedly builds ~4 Atlas a month against Hyundai's 30,000/yr goal for 2028. Epoch (Apr 2026) measures a 6-month production doubling for humanoids in 2022-2025 on a tiny base, finds high-precision reducers cap output near ~500k/yr today, and judges 1.5-3M/yr by end-2030 'clearly achievable' after a demand shock and 5-10M/yr 'plausible'.

Robots-build-robots versus the construction workforce (our stock model): U.S. construction worker-equivalents supplied by general-purpose robots in 2031 are ~3k (slow), ~60k (central, ~0.8% of ~8.3M U.S. construction workers) or ~530k (fast, ~6%); in 2035 ~30k, ~1.1M (~13%) or ~11M (more than the whole workforce). The central 2031 figure is about one-sixth of a single year's hiring need (ABC: 349k in 2026, 456k in 2027). By 2031 robots ease shortages at the margin; by 2035, in the central-to-fast paths, field labor stops binding and the critical path becomes institutions, equipment and physics.

The robot loop's own latency is an infrastructure gate: new factories take 6-9 months in China (usually 10-12) and 2+ years in most Western countries (Epoch 2026); Forethought's estimate of ~1-year robot doubling with abundant AI labor becomes 'on the order of a few years' in practice. Robot factories, their suppliers and the data centers that train them draw power from the same interconnection queues, so the loop competes with the infrastructure it is supposed to accelerate.

Where robotics bites hardest by 2031: earthwork and piling (calendar factor 0.5-0.7x), factory-built modules and power skids (already 12-18 months site-to-energization versus 24-36 stick-built, reported), U.S. fabs and factories (closing the ~2x U.S.-to-Taiwan gap, ~38 versus ~19 months, which is largely labor, 24/7 work and permitting), and repeat builds (the 3.4x spread between Japanese ABWRs at ~37 months to fuel load and Vogtle 3/4 at ~124 months is organizational and labor learning, not physics).

Speed provokes institutional backlash, which robots cannot fix and which can lengthen gates: Texas paused data-center interconnection approvals on Aug 3 2026 (ERCOT large-load requests ~474 GW, ~90% data centers) and on Sep 21 2026 froze all TCEQ data-center permits including behind-the-meter generation; xAI's Southaven turbines drew an NAACP Clean Air Act suit and an agreed order to remove all 69 temporary turbines by July 2027. In S4 the permit and politics share of the critical path rises from ~40% today to ~45-70%.

China shows the physical build rate is bounded by institutions and supply chains rather than by hands: it added 315 GW of solar and 119 GW of wind in 2025 and its fleet grew 16.1% to 3.89 TW, with no humanoids involved. The U.S. constraint on building faster is mostly not labor scarcity; S4 robotics therefore compresses the U.S. less than the narrative suggests, and compresses already-fast jurisdictions even less.

For the Space Unlock Tree, S4 moves only the infrastructure-type gates, and modestly by 2031: launch pad and propellant plant from 0.8-0.9x (S3) to 0.7-0.85x; production ramp from 0.7-0.8x to 0.6-0.7x; long-lead parts from 0.8-0.9x to 0.75-0.9x; NEPA, FAA and FCC gates unchanged. By 2035 these become 0.55-0.7x, 0.4-0.55x and 0.6-0.75x. The terrestrial gates that the orbital-compute thesis leans on (power interconnection, permits) remain institutional under S4 through 2031.

what_robotics_compresses: Earthwork, grading, trenching and pile driving: autonomous excavators, dozers and pile drivers working 24/7 give 2-3x per-machine output (Built ~3x piles/day; Bedrock operator-free since Aug 2026). Calendar factor 0.5-0.7x by 2031, 0.3-0.5x by 2035.

Repetitive interior and MEP tasks: layout (Dusty), overhead drilling (Jaibot 3-4x), drywall finishing (Canvas ~5 to ~2 days), rebar tying, painting, cable tray and conduit runs. Each is 2-4x on its own slice; on a whole fit-out the gain is ~1.2-1.5x by 2031.

Moving site labor into robot-staffed factories: prefabricated power skids, modular electrical rooms, MEP racks, precast and volumetric modules (12-18 months versus 24-36 to energization; modular 20-50% faster). Robots make these factory lines scale; this is the largest single lever before 2031.

Throughput of equipment factories (transformer winding and assembly, switchgear, turbine machining and assembly, welding), once robot-staffed capacity expansions are built; they arrive 2-3 years after the decision in the West.
Round-the-clock work: U.S. fabs and many Western sites are not built 24/7, which is a large part of the ~2x U.S.-to-Taiwan fab gap (~38 versus ~19 months).
Aggregate build rate (GW per year, sites in parallel) by relaxing the skilled-labor ceiling, especially electricians (45-70% of data center construction cost; ABC hiring need 349k in 2026).

Learning-curve losses on repeat builds: much of the 3.4x spread between Japanese ABWRs (~37 months) and Vogtle 3/4 (~124 months) is crew learning, rework and QA, which robot crews with AI documentation could narrow on standardized designs.
Inspection, progress monitoring, as-built verification and QA documentation (Spot, drones, scanning); these are cognitive gains mostly already counted in S3.
what_robotics_cannot_compress: Interconnection studies, cluster cycles and utility approvals (median 61 months request-to-operation for 2025 builds; ~4-7 years to connect a 100 MW load).

Permits, environmental review, litigation and political moratoria (EIS median 2.2 years; Texas data-center interconnection pause Aug 2026 and TCEQ permit freeze Sep 2026 including behind-the-meter; NAACP Clean Air Act suit over xAI turbines). Faster building can provoke longer institutional gates.
Siting, land rights and eminent domain for linear infrastructure (SunZia ~18 years; Grain Belt Express approved by Kansas in 2011 and still unbuilt; highways 9-19 years planning-to-construction).
Equipment queues where demand grows with AI: lead time = backlog / throughput, and S4 raises the backlog (GE Vernova ~5.8 years of output under contract; GSU transformer demand +274% 2019-2025).

Upstream materials and specialized-process capacity: grain-oriented electrical steel for transformers, single-crystal superalloy castings for turbine hot sections, EUV and other fab tools, copper and cement; new mines and mills take many years (general).

Physics time constants: concrete curing (28-day design strength; ~65-70% at 7 days, general), soil consolidation, transformer drying and impulse testing, cleanroom certification, fab tool qualification and yield ramp (~1 year), turbine full-load testing, nuclear hot functional testing, grid energization and protection testing.
The robot loop's own latency: robot and component factories take 6-12 months in China and 2+ years in the West, and draw power from the same queues as the infrastructure they would accelerate.
Capital approval, appropriations and financing for public infrastructure (highways, transmission, water), and ratepayer cost allocation for grid upgrades.
Weather, seasons and work-hour or noise ordinances that limit 24/7 operation near communities.

Adoption frictions specific to construction: a fragmented contractor base, building codes, inspection regimes, liability and union agreements (Hyundai's largest union demanded agreement before any robots are introduced).
timeline_view: 2026-2027: single-task robots (autonomous excavation and piling, layout, drilling, drywall) move from pilots to fleets of hundreds; humanoids do no trade work on sites. Calendar effect on whole projects ~0; the real accelerators are prefab modules, behind-the-meter power and permitting workarounds, and they are already provoking backlash (Texas, Southaven). 2028-2029: under S4, humanoid production reaches ~0.4-2M/yr worldwide, mostly into factories and logistics; robot-staffed lines for power skids, modular rooms and equipment begin to expand, but equipment queues stay long because AI demand is rising faster. Leading-edge sites see field-labor slices 1.3-1.6x faster. 2030-2031: robots supply roughly 0.8% (central) to 6% (fast) of U.S. construction labor; labor-bound gates run 0.5-0.75x on leading projects; a U.S. grid-connected project is ~21-28% shorter (versus ~19% in S3) and a permissive one ~21-31%; aggregate labor-limited build capacity rises ~1.1-1.5x. Institutions now hold ~40-45% of the remaining critical path. 2032-2035: if production keeps doubling every 10-16 months, robot labor reaches ~13% (central) to more than 100% (fast) of today's U.S. construction workforce, field labor stops binding, robot-built factories finally shrink transformer and turbine queues, and project calendars shorten ~38-54%. From then on, permitting, interconnection, physics time constants and politics are ~60-70% of what remains. Net: the robots-build-robots loop is too small by 2031 to change infrastructure calendars by much more than S3; it matters by 2035, and mainly for how much gets built rather than how fast one project finishes.
strongest_case_fast: The record already shows human-crewed builds running 3-12x faster than typical when capital and permission line up: Colossus 1 in 122 days; Colossus 2 to ~200 MW of cooling in ~5.5 months and ~0.85-0.9 GW of IT in ~15 months; Tesla Shanghai in 8 months; China adding 434 GW of wind and solar in one year. What stops this from being the norm in the U.S. is largely skilled labor (electricians are 45-70% of data center cost; 349-456k hires needed a year), 24/7 operation and equipment-factory throughput, and robots attack exactly these. Humanoid production doubled every ~6 months in 2022-2025, Epoch judges 5-10M/yr plausible by 2030 after a demand shock, and Forethought's industrial-explosion note puts robot self-replication near a 1-year doubling. Meanwhile the government is treating AI infrastructure as national security (DOJ intervening for xAI; EO 14335; FAST-41 and CITAP two-year federal clocks), so institutional gates may shrink too. Put together: by 2031 a 1 GW campus with on-site power could be energized in 6-9 months almost anywhere permissive; robot-staffed transformer and switchgear lines could halve lead times by 2030; and with labor no longer binding, aggregate U.S. build capacity could double, giving 35-45% shorter grid-connected projects by 2031 rather than 21-28%.
strongest_case_slow: Construction productivity has fallen for fifty years despite available machinery; the sector's fragmentation, uniqueness and regulation are exactly what slow robot adoption. Today's site robots are single-task, vendor-measured 2-4x gains on slivers of the critical path; autonomous haul trucks, in the most structured outdoor setting there is, took 18 years to reach 1,000 units. Humanoid output is ~19k per half-year, two-thirds of it non-productive, and Atlas is built at ~4 a month. The long poles are institutional (61-month interconnection, 4-7 year load connection, 18-year transmission lines, 9-19 year highways) and equipment queues in which AI demand grows faster than robot-boosted supply. Speed is already generating backlash: Texas froze data-center interconnection approvals and permits in Aug-Sep 2026, and xAI must remove 69 turbines after a Clean Air Act suit. On this view S4 adds 0-5 points of compression over S3 by 2031 (U.S. grid-connected projects ~19-22% shorter), robots mostly backfill retiring workers, and the loop matters only after 2035.

results.scenario: Ceiling: labor and equipment free, institutions and physics at S4-2031 levels

amdahl_infrastructure.reading: Robotics adds 2 (average) to 9 (leading-edge) points of compression over S3 by 2031 for U.S. grid-connected projects and 3-13 points for permissive ones. The binding share shifts to institutions (U.S.) or equipment queues (permissive). With labor and equipment made free, 2031 institutions and physics still cap the U.S. case at ~56% shorter.

robots_build_robots_loop.question: Can a robots-build-robots loop grow fast enough by 2031 (versus 2035) to matter for infrastructure build times?
robots_build_robots_loop.model: Global general-purpose robot production paths (M units/yr, 2026-2035): slow 0.06, 0.10, 0.18, 0.35, 0.6, 0.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0; central 0.06, 0.15, 0.35, 0.8, 1.8, 3.5, 6, 9, 12, 15; fast 0.06, 0.2, 0.6, 1.8, 5, 10, 18, 28, 40, 50. Five-year service life. Construction share of stock 3/6/10% in 2031 and 5/10/15% in 2035; U.S. share 10/20/25%; worker-equivalents per robot 0.5/0.8/1.2 in 2031 and 0.7/1.2/2.0 in 2035 (24/7 operation offsets lower dexterity). Denominator: ~8.3M U.S. construction workers (general). Central path is anchored on Epoch's post-shock 1.5-3M/yr by 2030; fast on Epoch's 5-10M/yr 'plausible'.
robots_build_robots_loop.verdict_2031: Too small to change infrastructure calendars much beyond S3. Central-path robot labor is ~1/6 of one year's U.S. construction hiring need; specialized single-task machines matter more than humanoids before 2031. Robots go to structured factories and warehouses first, and construction sites are the hardest environment (unstructured, outdoor, safety-critical).
robots_build_robots_loop.verdict_2035: Matters in the central and fast paths: field labor stops binding, robot-staffed equipment factories expand, and project calendars shorten 38-54%. The binding constraints become permits, interconnection, physics time constants and politics.
loop_latency_limits: Factory build latency: 6-9 months China (usually 10-12), 2+ years West (Epoch 2026)
High-precision reducers cap humanoids at ~500k/yr until new capacity is built (Epoch 2026)
Power for robot factories and training compute comes from the same interconnection and turbine queues
Forethought: ~1-year doubling with abundant AI labor in theory; 'on the order of a few years' in practice

mapping_to_space_model.note: Suggested S4 calendar-time factors for the infrastructure-type gates in the Space Unlock Tree physical-gate table (S3 values from the model).

rows.gate: Heavy launch pad and propellant plant
rows.why: Pads are concrete, steel, cryogenic plants and permits; robots compress civil, structural and MEP labor and allow 24/7 work; air-separation and compressor lead times and NEPA do not move.
New lines and factories are built faster and staffed by robots; factory build latency (2+ years in the U.S.) and tooling still bind.
Supplier throughput rises, but AI-driven demand for castings, forgings, electronics and power equipment rises too; lead time = backlog / throughput.

rows.gate: Environmental review (NEPA) for a new site or cadence
rows.why: Robots do not touch comment periods, consultation or litigation; any further gain is institutional.

rows.gate: Terrestrial AI compute campus (competitor to orbital compute)
rows.why: Robots speed the build but not interconnection or permits, so the 'speed to power' argument for orbital compute survives S4 through 2031.

signposts.event: Operator-free heavy equipment exceeds ~500 machines on U.S. sites (Bedrock, Gravis, Built, OEMs) by end-2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms earthwork and piling at 0.5-0.7x by 2031; below ~100 machines keeps them near 0.9x.

signposts.event: Humanoid shipments of >=200k in 2027 with >30% doing paid repeated work; Atlas output >=1,000/month by 2028
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves toward the central-to-fast robot-stock path; below ~100k in 2027 means the slow path.

signposts.event: First data center or fab with >=100 general-purpose robots doing electrical or mechanical trade work on one site (2028-2029)
signposts.what_it_changes: Turns the field-labor speedup from 1.4x (average) toward 2x for leading projects by 2031.

signposts.event: Wood Mackenzie transformer survey shows large-unit lead times below 100 weeks while demand is still rising
signposts.what_it_changes: Robot-staffed factory throughput is outrunning demand; equipment-queue factor moves from 0.8-1.0x toward 0.6-0.7x before 2031.

signposts.event: GE Vernova (or Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi) exceeds 30 GW/yr of gas turbine output before 2030 or reopens 2029-2030 slots
LBNL Queued Up 2027: median request-to-operation for 2026 builds below ~55 months, or above ~65 months
signposts.what_it_changes: Tests whether Order 2023 and AI-assisted studies are shrinking the institutional gate or whether the AI demand surge is lengthening it.

signposts.event: Texas ERCOT audit and TCEQ permit freeze (report due Oct 19 2026; audit expected mid-Dec 2026) and copycat moratoria in other states
signposts.what_it_changes: Lifting quickly supports institutional factors of 0.8x or better; spreading supports >1.0x on large-load connection under S4.

signposts.event: A 1 GW AI campus energized in under 9 months from groundbreaking
signposts.what_it_changes: Shows the best-practice frontier still moving; Colossus 2 at ~12-15 months is today's mark.

signposts.event: BLS or BEA construction labor productivity rises for three straight years
signposts.what_it_changes: First evidence that robotics and AI are breaking the 50-year stagnation, rather than only easing shortages.

signposts.event: TSMC Arizona Fab 3 or another U.S. fab builds permitting-to-production in <=24 months
signposts.what_it_changes: U.S. fabs closing on Taiwan's ~19 months; supports the U.S. fab factor of 0.65-0.8x by 2031.

data_quality_notes: Most construction-robot productivity figures are vendor claims without published methodology (Built, Dusty, Canvas, Hilti, ICON).
Humanoid counts conflict across Omdia, Counterpoint, SAG, Morgan Stanley and company statements; Tesla and Figure publish no unit counts.
LBNL 2026 edition values come from search summaries of the report (direct fetch returned 403); the 2025 edition values (55 months for 2024 builds) were corroborated.
The Wood Mackenzie 128/144-week figures come through trade press; the underlying survey was not accessed.
The Exyte fab comparison (19 vs 38 months) is from Tom's Hardware search excerpts; the article body could not be fetched.
Critical-path shares in the Amdahl table and the robot-stock parameters are this analysis's estimates, not sourced values.
